summary:
Santander is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework, whose formal provisions are among the most developed in the region. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended the change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Entry rules and partner recognition operate in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad receive the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presentation of a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to premises and dignified treatment in custody rest on specific court orders and decrees. Judgments T-314 of 2011 concerning the Tequendama Hotel, T-909 of 2011 concerning Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali and T-301 of 2004 concerning police at the Santa Marta boardwalk protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, while a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

The protection framework sits alongside lethal violence, none of it documented inside Santander in this inventory. On 5 April 2025 video of Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia was circulated online; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon, and no arrests had been made although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Her mother Sandra Borja said they killed her for being who she was. Hate killings claimed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier fatal attacks including gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed in his sleep, and victims killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Some targeting is organised and directed by armed groups. In Caquetá, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, a week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night, and she has since been forced to move twice. "Social cleansing" flyers appeared on Caquetá streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, 41 in 2023, and more than 40 in 2023 in separate counts cited elsewhere in the record. Discrimination limits trans women in the department mainly to hairdressing or sex work. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that all named people will be military targets including trans people.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's legal provisions and its recorded violence run in opposite directions, and the gap is documented rather than contested. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 assessment framed institutional reform and lived experience as divergent measures of the same country, with rising killings recorded during the same period that notary-based marker change and non-binary document markers took effect.

Violence cited in the record clusters in departments neighbouring or distant from Santander, principally Antioquia, Caquetá and Guajira, and is frequently perpetrated by armed groups operating outside the 2016 peace agreement. Trans women in the affected departments report displacement within Colombia itself, moving between towns after death threats, which suggests internal movement carries its own exposure.

Work exclusion compounds physical risk: where discrimination confines trans women to hairdressing or sex work, income depends on street presence and on clients met through apps or bars, the settings in which several of the recorded fatal attacks began. The pattern links labour market exclusion to the geography of the killings.

The killing totals in the record come from different counts and different periods, 41 in 2023 in one tally and more than 40 in 2023 in another, 8 between February and April 2024, 13 in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 recorded by the Attorney General's Office. They are not a single series and should not be read as one.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on their identification by signing a document before a notary, a process available nationwide since June 2015 and exercised in Santander through the same notarial offices that handle any other registry act. Non-binary markers have been available on national documents since November 2025.

Domestic partners and spouses hold the rights set out in national law regardless of the sex of the parties: marriage equality dates from 2016 and joint adoption from 2015, and couples whose marriage was performed abroad present their stamped certificate and identification at the nearest designated office to obtain recognition.

Institutions serving residents of Santander carry the procedural obligations set by the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree across public education, health care, prisons and victim assistance, and the May 2018 executive decree extends guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Residents placed in custody are covered by the rulings permitting trans detainees to maintain their own presentation and by the later court decision on the treatment of trans detainees.

Residents entering private premises have the protection of the Constitutional Court's T-314 of 2011, T-909 of 2011 and T-301 of 2004 judgments, which bind hotels, shopping centres and police in Santander on the same terms as elsewhere in the country.

Where threats or attacks occur, the record shows established channels: the Attorney General's Office logs LGBTI killings, the president can order urgent investigation, and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace has jurisdiction over conflict-related gender persecution. The record does not describe how these channels have performed inside Santander.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a trans-specific killing, arrest, legal restriction or facility dispute inside Santander. The violent incidents cited, the Millerey killing in Bello, Antioquia, the armed-group threats and flyer campaigns in Caquetá and Guajira, occurred in other departments, and the killing totals are national. Santander's position in this record is inferred from the national framework and from neighbouring-department patterns rather than from local evidence.

The frequency and form of police or municipal enforcement in Santander of the national rules on marker change, premises access and detention treatment is unresolved in this inventory. Whether Santander's notaries, hospitals and detention facilities apply the national procedures consistently is not sourced either way.

Two different counts for 2023 appear in the sources, 41 trans women killed and more than 40 killed, and their relationship is unresolved. The 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office for January to May 2025 and the 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 are drawn from different denominators and are not directly comparable.

Santander-specific data on housing, employment and health-care access for trans residents, including whether the May 2018 executive decree's guarantees are implemented locally, is not sourced here. The same is true for hate-crime charging rates and sentencing outcomes in the department.
